grammar.title: Descriptive language
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Adjetivos compostos** (duas palavras + hífen, antes do substantivo):
- **adjetivo/advérbio + particípio:** well-known, long-awaited, badly-paid, newly-built, highly-respected
- **substantivo + particípio:** sun-drenched, rain-soaked, home-made, hand-written, tear-stained
- **adjetivo + substantivo-ed:** blue-eyed, broken-hearted, open-minded, short-tempered, bad-tempered
- **substantivo/adjetivo + -ing:** heart-warming, record-breaking, mouth-watering, good-looking, never-ending
- **número + substantivo (singular!):** a **ten-minute** walk, a **five-star** hotel, a **two-hour** film

**2. Verbos expressivos** (mostram **como**):
- **walk:** stroll (sem pressa), stride (confiante), stagger (cambaleando), tiptoe (na ponta dos pés), wander (sem rumo), limp (mancando)
- **say:** whisper, mutter, mumble, yell, snap (irritado), sigh, stammer
- **look:** glance, stare, gaze (com admiração), peer (com dificuldade), glimpse
- **laugh:** giggle, chuckle, burst out laughing · **cry:** sob, weep

**3. Ordem dos adjetivos** (nativos seguem intuitivamente):
**opinião → tamanho → idade → forma → cor → origem → material → propósito + substantivo**
"a **lovely little old** **white** **Portuguese** **stone** cottage"
Na prática, use no máximo 2–3 adjetivos seguidos.

**4. "Show, don't tell"** — em vez de **dizer** a emoção, **mostre** com ações e detalhes:
- Tell: "She was nervous."
- Show: "She **glanced** at the clock for the third time, **twisting** her ring around her finger."

rows: a three-hour flight, a ten-year-old boy

examples.en: The long-awaited sequel turned out to be a gripping, beautifully-written novel.
examples.pt: A tão aguardada sequência acabou sendo um romance envolvente e lindamente escrito.

examples.en: He staggered into the kitchen, rain-soaked and exhausted, and muttered an apology.
examples.pt: Ele entrou cambaleando na cozinha, encharcado e exausto, e resmungou um pedido de desculpas.

examples.en: We rented a charming little whitewashed fisherman's cottage near the beach.
examples.pt: Alugamos uma charmosa casinha caiada de pescador perto da praia.

grammar.tip_pt: Erro clássico: "a ten-**minutes** walk". Em adjetivos compostos com número, o substantivo fica **no singular**: a ten-**minute** walk, a five-**year**-old girl, a two-**hour** meeting.

common_mistakes.wrong: It's a five-minutes walk from here.
common_mistakes.right: It's a five-minute walk from here.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Adjetivo composto com número: substantivo no singular.

common_mistakes.wrong: She was very very sad and she cried a lot.
common_mistakes.right: Her shoulders shook as she sobbed quietly into her hands.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Show, don't tell: verbos precisos em vez de intensificadores repetidos.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em geral, adjetivos compostos têm acento **nas duas partes**, com o mais forte na **segunda**: well-**KNOWN**, long-a**WAI**ted, home-**MADE**. Mas antes de um substantivo, o acento pode mudar para a primeira parte: a **WELL**-known **AC**tor.

dialogue.title: Writing workshop
dialogue.context_pt: Uma professora de escrita criativa dá feedback a um aluno sobre o início de um conto.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Read me your first line again, Caio.
lines.pt: Leia de novo sua primeira frase, Caio.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: "The man walked into the bar. He was sad because his wife had left him."
lines.pt: "O homem entrou no bar. Ele estava triste porque a esposa o tinha deixado."

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: OK. The information's there, but it's telling, not showing. How did he walk in?
lines.pt: OK. A informação está lá, mas você está contando, não mostrando. Como ele entrou?

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: Slowly, I suppose. Tired.
lines.pt: Devagar, acho. Cansado.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: So find a verb that does that work. Did he stagger? Trudge? Drag himself?
lines.pt: Então encontre um verbo que faça esse trabalho. Ele cambaleou? Se arrastou?

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: "The man trudged into the half-empty bar and slumped onto a stool."
lines.pt: "O homem entrou arrastando os pés no bar meio vazio e desabou num banquinho."

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Much better! Now, instead of saying he's sad, show me a detail.
lines.pt: Muito melhor! Agora, em vez de dizer que ele está triste, me mostre um detalhe.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: "He turned his wedding ring round and round, staring at the empty seat beside him."
lines.pt: "Ele girava a aliança sem parar, olhando fixamente para o lugar vazio ao lado."

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Now that's a story I want to keep reading. You don't need to tell me his wife left — I can feel it.
lines.pt: Agora sim, essa é uma história que eu quero continuar lendo. Você não precisa me dizer que a esposa foi embora — eu sinto.

listening.title: Why our brains love stories
listening.context_pt: Um neurocientista explica, num podcast, como o cérebro reage a histórias.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Why do stories grip us so powerfully? Part of the answer may lie in the brain. When we read a list of facts, the areas involved in processing language become active. But a number of studies have suggested that vivid descriptions can engage other areas too. In one experiment, words with strong smell associations, like "coffee" or "perfume", appeared to activate regions linked to the sense of smell. Metaphors involving texture — "a rough day", "a velvety voice" — seemed to engage areas related to touch. Researchers are cautious about these findings, and brain-imaging studies are notoriously difficult to interpret. But they're consistent with something writers have always known: a well-told story isn't just understood, it's experienced. That's also why stories are remembered so much better than statistics. Tell people that thousands of children are hungry, and they nod. Tell them about one child — her name, her face, what she had for breakfast — and they act.

questions.q: What happens in the brain when we read a list of facts?
questions.answer: The language-processing areas become active.

questions.q: What did words like "coffee" appear to activate?
questions.answer: Regions linked to the sense of smell.

questions.q: Why are researchers cautious?
questions.answer: Brain-imaging studies are notoriously difficult to interpret.

questions.q: Why are stories more effective than statistics?
questions.answer: People connect with an individual story and act; statistics just make them nod.

reading.title: Six words
reading.text: "For sale: baby shoes, never worn." These six words are often described as the shortest story ever written, and they are frequently attributed to Ernest Hemingway, who is said to have written them to win a bet. There is, however, no reliable evidence that he did; similar newspaper adverts had appeared years before. Whoever wrote it, the story is a perfect illustration of a principle at the heart of good writing: what is left out can be as powerful as what is put in. The reader is never told what happened. There is no description of grief, no explanation, no ending. And yet most readers feel a sudden, heart-breaking weight. The story works precisely because the reader's imagination does the work. Hemingway himself described a similar idea, sometimes called the "iceberg theory": a writer who knows his subject well can omit much of it, and the reader will still sense what lies beneath the surface. Many writing teachers express the same idea with the phrase "show, don't tell". Rather than stating that a character is lonely, a writer might describe him setting the table for two out of habit, then slowly putting one plate away. Rather than declaring that a city is poor, she might describe children playing football with a ball made of plastic bags. Of course, the rule can be overused. Sometimes the clearest, most efficient choice is simply to tell. But the six-word story reminds us of something worth remembering in any kind of writing, from novels to emails: readers are not passive recipients of information. Given the right details, they will build the world themselves.

questions.q: Is there evidence that Hemingway wrote the six-word story?
questions.answer: No reliable evidence; similar adverts had appeared before.

questions.q: Why does the story work?
questions.answer: The reader's imagination does the work; what is left out is powerful.

questions.q: What is the "iceberg theory"?
questions.answer: A writer can omit much of what they know, and the reader will sense what lies beneath.

questions.q: Give one example of "showing" from the text.
questions.answer: A man setting the table for two, then putting one plate away / children playing with a ball of plastic bags.

writing.model:
The letter

Nobody noticed the letter for three days.

It lay face down on the dusty hall table, half-hidden beneath a pile of pizza menus and electricity bills. The Oliveiras were a busy, fast-moving family: Paulo strode out of the house at six every morning, his phone already pressed to his ear; Cláudia rushed the twins to school, a half-eaten piece of toast in one hand; and sixteen-year-old Bia drifted in and out like a ghost, earphones permanently in place.

It was Dona Lurdes, the grandmother, who finally found it. She had shuffled into the hall on Thursday evening, searching for her reading glasses, when she glimpsed the familiar handwriting on the envelope. Her hands began to tremble.

She lowered herself slowly onto the stairs and peered at the faded stamp. Portugal. The postmark was three weeks old.

For a long time she simply sat there, turning the envelope over and over, as if it might disappear. Upstairs, a door slammed. Somewhere, a television roared with recorded laughter.

When Cláudia came looking for her, she found her mother-in-law still sitting on the bottom step, the letter open on her lap, tear-stained but smiling.

"Dona Lurdes? What's wrong?"

The old woman didn't answer at first. She smoothed out the thin, hand-written pages and pointed to the signature at the bottom.

"Fernando," she whispered. "My brother. I haven't heard his voice in fifty-two years."

Cláudia sat down beside her. Neither of them spoke. In the kitchen, the dinner was burning, and for once, nobody cared.

Later that night, the whole family gathered around the dining table — even Bia, who had taken her earphones out — while Dona Lurdes read the letter aloud. It was a long, rambling, heart-warming account of a life lived on the other side of the ocean: a fishing boat, a wife, four children, eleven grandchildren.

At the end, there was a phone number.

grammar.title: Word formation
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Prefixos negativos** (o contrário):
- **un-**: unpredictable, unconvincing, unforgettable, unrealistic
- **in-**: inaccurate, incomplete, insensitive
- **im-** (antes de m, p, b): impossible, impatient, immature
- **ir-** (antes de r): irrelevant, irresistible, irresponsible
- **il-** (antes de l): illogical, illegal, illiterate
- **dis-**: dishonest, dislike, disappointing, disagree
- **non-**: non-fiction, non-existent

**2. Prefixos de sentido:**
- **mis-** (errado): misunderstand, misinterpret, miscast, mislead
- **over- / under-** (demais / de menos): overrated / underrated, overpriced, underestimate
- **re-** (de novo): remake, reread, reinvent
- **out-** (superar): outperform, outsell, outlive
- **counter-** (contra): counterproductive, counterpart
- **co-**: co-star, co-writer

**3. Sufixos que formam substantivos:**
- **-ness**: darkness, awareness, effectiveness
- **-ity**: originality, creativity, popularity, authenticity
- **-ment**: disappointment, achievement, entertainment
- **-tion/-sion**: production, adaptation, tension
- **-ance/-ence**: performance, relevance, existence
- **-ship / -hood**: relationship, childhood

**4. Sufixos que formam adjetivos:**
- **-able/-ible**: predictable, forgettable, believable, incredible
- **-ive**: impressive, creative, repetitive
- **-ful / -less**: powerful, pointless, meaningless
- **-ous**: ambitious, humorous, glamorous
- **-al / -ic**: emotional, dramatic, iconic

**5. Sufixos que formam verbos e advérbios:**
- **-ize/-ise**: dramatize, criticize, romanticize · **-en**: strengthen, shorten · **-ify**: intensify, simplify
- **-ly**: surprisingly, unexpectedly, convincingly

**Dica de prova:** leia a frase toda e pergunte: preciso de **substantivo, adjetivo, verbo ou advérbio**? **Positivo ou negativo**? **Singular ou plural**?

examples.en: Despite its huge popularity, the series was criticized for its unrealistic dialogue.
examples.pt: Apesar da enorme popularidade, a série foi criticada pelos diálogos irrealistas.

examples.en: The remake is surprisingly faithful to the original, but it lacks originality.
examples.pt: O remake é surpreendentemente fiel ao original, mas falta originalidade.

examples.en: Critics completely underestimated the film, which went on to outperform every other release that year.

grammar.tip_pt: Cuidado com os prefixos negativos que **não** seguem o português: **in**ac**cur**ate (impreciso), **un**able (incapaz), **dis**honest (desonesto), **un**comfortable (desconfortável), **ir**responsible. Na dúvida, consulte o dicionário — e anote a família inteira.

common_mistakes.wrong: The ending was a big deception.
common_mistakes.right: The ending was a big disappointment.

pronunciation.tip_pt: O acento se move com os sufixos: **CRI**tic → **CRI**ticize → criti**CIS**m? Não! **CRI**ticism. Mas: o**RI**ginal → origi**NA**lity; **PHO**tograph → pho**TO**graphy → photo**GRA**phic; pre**DICT** → pre**DIC**table. Sufixos como **-ity, -ic, -ion** puxam o acento para a sílaba anterior.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.en: So? What did you think? I thought it was unforgettable!

lines.speaker: Vini
lines.en: Honestly? I found it hugely overrated. Everyone kept saying it was a masterpiece, but the plot was completely predictable.

lines.speaker: Bel

lines.speaker: Vini
lines.en: I saw it coming from the first scene. And the lead actor was miscast. He's too young for the role — it was a bit unconvincing.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.en: I disagree. I thought his performance was incredibly powerful, especially in the courtroom scene.

lines.speaker: Vini

lines.speaker: Bel

lines.pt: Viu? Você gostou mais do que está admitindo. Só está sendo crítico demais porque todo mundo ama.

lines.speaker: Vini

listening.title: Can we trust online ratings?
listening.context_pt: Um especialista em mídia fala sobre avaliações online de filmes e séries.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Before watching a film, millions of people check a score — the percentage of positive reviews on an aggregator site, or the star rating on a streaming platform. These numbers are useful, but they can be misleading. First, a high percentage doesn't necessarily mean a film is outstanding; it means most critics found it at least acceptable. A film that nobody loves but nobody hates can score higher than a bold, divisive masterpiece. Second, audience ratings can be manipulated. There have been well-documented cases of "review bombing", in which groups of users deliberately flood a film with negative ratings, sometimes before it has even been released. And third, critics and audiences often disagree. Some films are critically acclaimed but commercially unsuccessful; others are box-office hits that critics dismiss. My advice? Don't rely on a single number. Read two or three reviews from critics whose taste you know — and remember that disagreement is part of the pleasure of art.

questions.q: What does a high percentage on an aggregator site mean?
questions.answer: Most critics found the film at least acceptable — not necessarily outstanding.

questions.q: Why can a divisive masterpiece score lower?
questions.answer: A film nobody loves or hates can get more positive reviews overall.

questions.q: What is "review bombing"?
questions.answer: Groups deliberately flooding a film with negative ratings.

questions.q: What is the speaker's advice?
questions.answer: Don't rely on a single number; read reviews from critics whose taste you know.

reading.title: In defence of the bad review
reading.text: In an age of star ratings and thumbs-up icons, the traditional film critic can seem like an endangered species. Many newspapers have reduced their arts coverage, and audiences increasingly rely on algorithms and influencers to decide what to watch. Some argue that critics have become irrelevant — or worse, that they are snobbish gatekeepers out of touch with what ordinary people enjoy. It is worth defending them, however, and especially their least popular product: the negative review. A thoughtful bad review is not simply an expression of dislike. At its best, it is an explanation — of why a story feels unconvincing, why a performance seems mechanical, why a film that cost hundreds of millions to make leaves no lasting impression. In explaining their disappointment, critics help readers understand what makes art work, and sharpen their own judgement in the process. Negative reviews also perform a useful function in an industry dominated by marketing. Studios spend enormous sums persuading audiences that every release is unmissable. Independent criticism offers a counterweight to that pressure, reminding us that our time and money are limited. Of course, criticism can be unfair, careless or simply cruel. A review that ridicules without explaining contributes little. And critics are not infallible: history is full of works that were dismissed on release and later recognized as masterpieces. But the solution to bad criticism is better criticism, not none at all. In the end, a culture in which everything is "amazing" is a culture in which nothing is. The willingness to say "this doesn't work, and here's why" may be one of the most valuable things a critic can offer.

questions.q: Why can critics seem like an endangered species?
questions.answer: Newspapers have reduced arts coverage, and audiences rely on algorithms and influencers.

questions.q: What is a thoughtful bad review, at its best?
questions.answer: An explanation of why something doesn't work.

questions.q: What function do negative reviews perform against marketing?
questions.answer: They offer a counterweight to studios' pressure that every release is unmissable.

questions.q: What does the final sentence mean: "a culture in which everything is amazing is a culture in which nothing is"?

writing.model:
Review: City of the Tides (series, season 1)

There has been no shortage of hype around City of the Tides, the new eight-episode Brazilian thriller set in a fictional fishing town on the coast of Bahia. Expectations were high, and for the most part, the series lives up to them.

The story follows Inês, a marine biologist who returns to her childhood home after twenty years to investigate the mysterious disappearance of a research boat. What begins as a straightforward mystery gradually develops into a thought-provoking drama about memory, family loyalty and the environmental destruction of the coast.

The series' greatest strength is its atmosphere. The photography is breathtaking: sun-drenched beaches and storm-darkened skies create a sense of beauty that is constantly threatened. The lead actress gives a remarkably powerful performance, conveying her character's guilt and determination with impressive subtlety. The supporting cast is equally convincing, particularly the actor playing her estranged father.

Unfortunately, the series is not without its weaknesses. The middle episodes are overlong and somewhat repetitive, and a subplot involving a corrupt politician feels underdeveloped and, at times, frankly unbelievable. Some viewers may also find the final twist a little predictable — although, to be fair, it is handled with considerable emotional intensity.

Despite these flaws, City of the Tides is an ambitious and genuinely original piece of television. It avoids the temptation to oversimplify its themes, and it trusts its audience to draw their own conclusions. The cliffhanger at the end of the final episode makes a second season almost irresistible.

Verdict: not quite the masterpiece some critics have claimed, but a gripping, beautifully made series that deserves a wide international audience. Definitely worth a binge-watch.

Rating: ★★★★☆

grammar.title: Comment adverbs and attitude
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Comment adverbs** (ou **sentence adverbs**) comentam a **frase inteira**, mostrando sua atitude. Geralmente vêm **no início**, seguidos de vírgula.

**1. Honestidade / franqueza:** frankly, honestly, to be honest, candidly, quite frankly
"**Frankly**, the show was a waste of money."

**2. Concessão:** admittedly, granted, of course, to be fair
"**Admittedly**, the jokes were a bit old. **To be fair**, the audience loved them."

**3. Opinião / grau de certeza:** arguably (possivelmente — defensável), apparently, presumably, supposedly (supostamente — com dúvida), undoubtedly, evidently, clearly
"It is **arguably** the funniest series of the decade."

**4. Reação emocional:** surprisingly, unsurprisingly, ironically, fortunately, sadly, luckily, oddly / strangely enough, predictably, understandably
"**Ironically**, the comedian who mocked technology became famous on TikTok."

**5. Óbvio:** needless to say, obviously, naturally, of course
"**Needless to say**, I never told that joke again."

**Understatement** (dizer menos do que se quer dizer) — típico do humor britânico:
- "It was **a bit** chilly." (= estava congelando)
- "He's **not the most** patient person." (= ele é muito impaciente)
- "That **could have gone better**." (= foi um desastre)
- "**Not bad**" pode significar "muito bom" — o tom decide.

**Ironia verbal** = dizer o contrário do que se pensa, geralmente com tom marcado:
- (Durante uma tempestade) "**Lovely** weather for a picnic!"
- **Sarcasmo** = ironia com intenção de criticar ou ferir: "Oh, **great** job, really."

⚠️ Ironia e sarcasmo **não funcionam bem por escrito** sem contexto — em e-mails profissionais, evite!

To be fair, it was his first show.

grammar.tip_pt: **Arguably** NÃO é "discutivelmente" no sentido negativo! Significa "**pode-se argumentar que / possivelmente**": "It's **arguably** the best film" = muitos diriam que é o melhor. E **eventually** ≠ eventualmente (= finalmente).

common_mistakes.why_pt: Arguably reforça uma opinião defensável, não a põe em dúvida.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Needless to say + frase direta, sem but.

common_mistakes.right: Ironically, the weather forecaster got caught in the storm.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Ironically = uma contradição inesperada, não só falta de sorte.

pronunciation.tip_pt: A ironia em inglês costuma vir com entonação **exagerada** ou **completamente plana** (deadpan): "Oh, **lovely** weather." (tom plano) / "**Great**. Just **great**." Understatement britânico é dito de forma **calma e neutra** — e é isso que o torna engraçado.

listening.title: Is humour universal?
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre humor em diferentes culturas.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: Laughter itself appears to be universal. Babies laugh long before they can speak, and researchers have observed play vocalizations resembling laughter in apes and other animals. But what people find funny varies enormously. British humour, for instance, is famous for understatement and irony. Saying "It's a bit damp" during a flood is, for many Britons, both funny and polite. Many Americans, by contrast, are often described as preferring a more direct, energetic style. In Brazil, humour is frequently warm and teasing, and it's often used to cope with difficult situations — there's a long tradition of making jokes about politics, inflation and everyday frustrations. Interestingly, what travels best across cultures tends to be physical comedy. Charlie Chaplin and Mr. Bean are loved almost everywhere, partly because they don't depend on words. Puns and wordplay, on the other hand, are notoriously difficult to translate. So, if you want to be funny in another language, my advice is: start with self-deprecation and situations people recognize, and save the puns for later.

questions.q: What evidence suggests laughter is universal?
questions.answer: Babies laugh before they speak, and animals like apes make laughter-like sounds.

questions.q: What is British humour famous for?
questions.answer: Understatement and irony.

questions.q: How is Brazilian humour described?

questions.q: What type of comedy travels best, and why?
questions.answer: Physical comedy, because it doesn't depend on words.

reading.title: The serious science of humour
reading.text: Why do we laugh? For a phenomenon so familiar, humour has proved surprisingly difficult to explain. Philosophers have offered several theories over the centuries. The oldest, associated with Plato and Thomas Hobbes, is the "superiority theory": we laugh at the misfortunes or foolishness of others because it makes us feel superior. This arguably explains slapstick and some teasing, but it hardly accounts for a clever pun. A second explanation, the "relief theory", linked to Sigmund Freud among others, suggests that laughter releases nervous energy or suppressed feelings — which may explain why people sometimes laugh at funerals or after a frightening experience. The most widely discussed today, however, is the "incongruity theory": we laugh when something violates our expectations in a way that makes sense on second thought. A punchline works because it forces us to reinterpret what came before. More recently, the researchers Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren proposed what they call the "benign violation theory". According to this idea, something is funny when it is simultaneously wrong in some way — a violation of how things should be — and yet harmless, or benign. Tickling is a good illustration: a mild physical "attack" that is clearly not dangerous. The theory also helps explain why a joke can fail in two opposite ways. If it is too safe, it is boring; if the violation feels too real or too painful, it is offensive. Needless to say, no theory captures everything. Humour depends heavily on context, culture and timing, and attempts to analyse a joke tend, ironically, to kill it. As the American writer E. B. White reportedly put it, analysing humour is like dissecting a frog: few people are interested, and the frog dies.

questions.q: What does the superiority theory claim?
questions.answer: We laugh at others' misfortunes because it makes us feel superior.

questions.q: What does the incongruity theory claim?
questions.answer: We laugh when expectations are violated in a way that makes sense on second thought.

questions.q: What is the benign violation theory?
questions.answer: Something is funny when it is wrong in some way but harmless.

questions.q: In what two ways can a joke fail, according to this theory?
questions.answer: It can be too safe (boring) or too painful (offensive).

writing.model:
Is anything off-limits in comedy?

Few debates generate as much heat, and, ironically, as little laughter, as the question of what comedians should be allowed to joke about. Every few months, a comedian somewhere is accused of crossing a line, and the same arguments are repeated: either we are "too sensitive" or comedians are "punching down".

Admittedly, comedy has always depended on taking risks. Many of the most celebrated comedians in history became famous precisely because they said things others didn't dare to. Satire, in particular, has long been one of the few weapons ordinary people have against the powerful. Unsurprisingly, authoritarian governments tend to have very little tolerance for jokes about themselves.

To be fair, however, freedom to joke is not the same as freedom from criticism. If a comedian makes a joke that audiences find cruel, they are entitled to say so — and to stop buying tickets. That is not censorship; it is feedback. Frankly, the comedians who complain loudest about "cancel culture" often seem to have more media attention than ever.

What matters, arguably, is not the topic itself but the target. Joking about a tragedy is not necessarily wrong; joking at the expense of its victims usually is. Some of the funniest comedy I've seen dealt with illness, grief and racism — but the people being laughed at were the powerful, the absurd or the comedian themselves, not those already suffering.

Needless to say, there will never be a rulebook that everyone agrees on. Humour depends on context, timing and trust between performer and audience. A joke that works in a small comedy club may fall flat on social media, where context disappears.

So, is anything off-limits? Perhaps not in principle. But a comedian who ignores the difference between laughing with people and laughing at them is, to put it mildly, not doing their job very well.

culture_note.title: Humor britânico x brasileiro
culture_note.text_pt: O humor britânico é famoso por **ironia, understatement e autodepreciação** (pense em *Monty Python* ou *The Office* britânico). Uma dica: quando um britânico diz **"That's very brave"** sobre sua ideia, pode ser que ele ache a ideia péssima!

grammar.title: Advanced cleft sentences
grammar.explanation_pt:
Cleft sentences dividem uma frase em duas partes para **destacar** uma informação. Revisão: "**What** I need **is** a break." / "**It was** Ana **who** called."

**1. What-cleft com ações (do / happen):**
- "**What she did was** (to) leave the room." (destaca a ação)
- "**What happened was (that)** the alarm went off."
- "**What I'd do is** call the gallery directly."

**2. All-cleft** (= a única coisa, só):
- "**All I want is** an honest opinion." / "**All he did was** sign his name."
- "**All** you need to do **is** ask."

**3. Substantivos gerais + cleft:**
- **The thing (that)... is**: "**The thing that** annoys me **is** the price."
- **The reason (why)... is that**: "**The reason** it's famous **is that** it was stolen."
- **The person who / The place where / The day when / The way**: "**The place where** you really see her talent **is** in her drawings."
- **Where / When / Why / How** sem antecedente: "**Where** the film works **is** in its silences." / "**How** he did it **is** a mystery."

**4. It's not that... it's (just) that...** (corrigir um mal-entendido):
- "**It's not that** I hate modern art; **it's just that** some of it feels empty."
- "**It isn't** the price **that** bothers me; **it's** the attitude."

**5. Cleft reverso** (a informação destacada vem primeiro):
- "A good night's sleep **is what** I need." / "That**'s why** I left." / "That**'s where** we disagree."

**Fala informal:** "**The thing is**, ..." / "**What happened was**, ..." são muito comuns como **marcadores de discurso**.

dialogue.title: At the art museum
dialogue.context_pt: Duas amigas visitam uma exposição de arte contemporânea e discordam sobre uma obra.

lines.speaker: Jade
lines.en: OK, I need you to explain this one to me. It's a white canvas. With one black line.
lines.pt: OK, preciso que você me explique esta. É uma tela branca. Com uma linha preta.

lines.speaker: Isa
lines.en: Ha! I knew you'd hate it.
lines.pt: Ha! Eu sabia que você ia odiar.

lines.speaker: Jade
lines.en: It's not that I hate it. It's just that I don't see why it's in a museum. All the artist did was draw a line!
lines.pt: Não é que eu odeie. É só que não entendo por que está num museu. Tudo o que o artista fez foi traçar uma linha!

lines.speaker: Isa
lines.en: But what makes it interesting is the context. The label says she made it after losing her sight in one eye. The line is what she could still see clearly.
lines.pt: Mas o que torna interessante é o contexto. A legenda diz que ela fez depois de perder a visão de um olho. A linha é o que ela ainda conseguia ver com clareza.

lines.speaker: Jade
lines.en: Oh. OK, that does change things a bit. The thing is, though, shouldn't art speak for itself, without a label?
lines.pt: Ah. OK, isso muda um pouco as coisas. Mas a questão é: a arte não deveria falar por si mesma, sem legenda?

lines.speaker: Isa
lines.en: Some art does. But where conceptual art really works is in making you ask questions — exactly like you're doing now.
lines.pt: Algumas obras falam. Mas onde a arte conceitual realmente funciona é em fazer você perguntar coisas — exatamente como você está fazendo agora.

lines.speaker: Jade
lines.en: Fine. All I'm saying is that I'd rather look at a Tarsila than a line.
lines.pt: Tá bom. Só estou dizendo que prefiro olhar um Tarsila do que uma linha.

lines.speaker: Isa
lines.en: That's fair. And that's why there's a Tarsila room next door. Come on!
lines.pt: Justo. E é por isso que tem uma sala da Tarsila aqui do lado. Vamos!

listening.title: The painting that shredded itself
listening.context_pt: Uma repórter relata um dos episódios mais famosos do mercado de arte recente.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.en: In October 2018, at an auction at Sotheby's in London, a framed copy of Banksy's Girl with Balloon was sold for just over one million pounds. What happened next stunned the room. Moments after the hammer came down, an alarm sounded and the canvas began to slide through a shredder hidden inside the frame. Halfway through, the shredder stopped. Banksy later posted a video suggesting that he had built the device years earlier, in case the work was ever put up for auction. Many people assumed the stunt would destroy the painting's value. What it actually did was the opposite. The half-shredded work was renamed Love is in the Bin, and in 2021 it was sold again — this time for more than eighteen million pounds. The reason it became so valuable is that the shredding itself became part of the artwork, and, arguably, part of art history. It's not that the art market missed the joke; it's that the market turned the joke into a product.

questions.q: What happened just after the painting was sold in 2018?
questions.answer: A hidden shredder in the frame began to shred the canvas.

questions.q: Why had Banksy built the device, according to his video?
questions.answer: In case the work was ever put up for auction.

questions.q: What was the work renamed, and what did it sell for in 2021?
questions.answer: Love is in the Bin; more than eighteen million pounds.

questions.q: What is the reporter's final point?
questions.answer: The market turned the joke into a product.

reading.title: What is art worth?
reading.text: In 2019, at the Art Basel fair in Miami, the Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan exhibited a work called Comedian: a real banana, attached to a wall with grey duct tape. Editions of the work were reportedly sold for around 120,000 dollars each. Then, to the delight of photographers, a performance artist peeled the banana off the wall and ate it. The gallery was unconcerned. What the buyers had purchased, it explained, was not the fruit itself but a certificate of authenticity and instructions for replacing it. The episode provoked a familiar mixture of laughter and outrage. For many people, it confirmed their suspicion that contemporary art is a joke played on the rich. Yet the story raises a serious question: where does the value of art actually lie? It is not that the materials of most great art are especially precious; paint, canvas and stone are relatively cheap. What we pay for, arguably, is something less tangible: an idea, a reputation, a story, a moment in history. Vincent van Gogh is often said to have sold only one painting in his lifetime — an oversimplification, but one that captures how little his work was valued while he lived. Today, his paintings rank among the most expensive ever sold. Nothing about the canvases changed. What changed was how people saw them. None of this means that every expensive work is a masterpiece, or that every unknown artist is a misunderstood genius. Markets can be driven by fashion, speculation and the desire for status. But perhaps the banana on the wall was doing exactly what art has always done: making us look again at something ordinary and ask what it means. The thing is, whether that is worth 120,000 dollars is a question no theory can answer for us.

questions.q: What did the buyers of Comedian actually purchase?
questions.answer: A certificate of authenticity and instructions for replacing the banana.

questions.q: What, according to the writer, do we really pay for in art?
questions.answer: Something intangible: an idea, a reputation, a story, a moment in history.

questions.q: What point does the van Gogh example make?
questions.answer: The canvases didn't change; what changed was how people saw them.

questions.q: What might the banana have been doing, according to the writer?
questions.answer: Making us look again at something ordinary and ask what it means.

writing.task: Write an article (280–320 words) for a cultural website titled "Why I changed my mind about..." (a type of art, music, a film genre or an artist). Use at least six advanced cleft sentences.
writing.task_pt: Escreva um artigo (280–320 palavras) para um site cultural intitulado "Por que mudei de ideia sobre..." (um tipo de arte, música, gênero de filme ou artista). Use pelo menos seis cleft sentences avançadas.
writing.model:
Why I changed my mind about contemporary art

For years, my opinion of contemporary art could be summed up in one sentence: "My nephew could have done that." It's not that I disliked art in general — I loved Renaissance paintings and the bright, bold canvases of Tarsila do Amaral. It's just that I couldn't see the point of empty rooms, piles of bricks or a single line on a white wall.

What changed my mind was a weekend at Inhotim, the enormous art park in Minas Gerais, a few years ago. I went reluctantly, mainly because a friend had already bought the tickets.

The first surprise was the setting. Instead of white walls and silent guards, what I found were tropical gardens, lakes and pavilions hidden among the trees. The thing that struck me most, though, was how differently I felt when I wasn't being told what to think.

One installation in particular stayed with me. All it consisted of was a dark room and a sound recording of the earth itself. I had no idea what I was supposed to understand. What I actually did was sit there for twenty minutes, completely absorbed, feeling something I couldn't name.

That's when I realized what I'd been getting wrong. I'd been treating contemporary art like a puzzle with a correct answer, and getting annoyed when I couldn't solve it. Where it really works, I think, is in creating an experience rather than delivering a message.

I still don't like everything, of course. Some works seem to me pretentious, and the prices at international auctions are, frankly, absurd. But the reason I keep going back to galleries now is that I've stopped asking "What does it mean?" and started asking "What does it do to me?"

My nephew, incidentally, is now studying fine art. Perhaps he could have done it after all.

culture_note.title: Inhotim e a Semana de 22
culture_note.text_pt: **Inhotim**, em Brumadinho (MG), é um dos maiores museus de arte contemporânea a céu aberto do mundo, conhecido internacionalmente. A **Semana de Arte Moderna de 1922**, em São Paulo, com nomes como Tarsila do Amaral, Anita Malfatti e Oswald de Andrade, é um marco da arte moderna brasileira. O **Abaporu**, de Tarsila, é frequentemente citado como uma das obras mais valiosas da arte brasileira.
